 Claiming age shapes your monthly check far more than most retirees realize.
 By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 9, 2026 at 6:00AM EST + Fool.com on Share Summarize with AI Key Points
 Retirees in their 70s receive a weighted average of $2,194.02 per month, which is $316.20 more than the $1,877.82 average for those in their 60s. 
 The SSA calculates your benefit based on your 35 highest-earning years, yet it is designed to replace only 40% of pre-retirement income. 
 Claiming at 62 can result in a permanent reduction of up to 30% for those with a full retirement age of 67. 
 You likely view Social Security through the lens of a single choice, like claiming at 62 or 67. Looking at it by decade reveals a more complete picture of how timing shapes the checks people actually receive.
 Viewing these figures as bands shows that your benefit isn't a fixed destination. It is the result of your work history and the age you chose to stop waiting.
 Image source: Getty Images.
 The average benefit by decade
 According to the Social Security Administration (SSA), the weighted average for beneficiaries in their 60s is $1,877.82 per month. For those in their 70s, the average increases to $2,194.02 as of December 2025, the most recent data available. This monthly gap of $316.20 adds up to about $3,794.40 per year.
 The SSA bases your benefit on an average of your wages across your 35 highest-earning years. Earlier wages are adjusted for inflation and run through the primary insurance amount (PIA) formula.
 Social Security is supplemental income. It was designed to replace only 40% of pre-retirement earnings, which is well short of what most retirees need. The benefit formula is the same for everyone.
 Age band Average monthly benefit 
 Your 60s (ages 62-69) $1,877.82 
 Your 70s (ages 70-79) $2,194.02 
 Why the averages shift in your 70s
 The difference between these decades likely reflects who is in each group. The 70s band likely includes more workers who waited for delayed retirement credits , worth 8% per year. These credits increase your benefit for every year you delay past full retirement age (FRA), up to age 70.
 Full retirement age ranges from 66 to 67, depending on your birth year, and it's 67 for everyone born in 1960 or later. If your FRA is 67, delaying until 70 earns you a 24% increase. For a worker with an FRA of 66, delaying until 70 yields a 32% increase.
 Conversely, many people in their 60s likely claimed at 62, the earliest claiming age. For someone with an FRA of 67, this results in a permanent 30% reduction. Those with an FRA of 66 see a 25% reduction in benefits when claiming at 62.
 A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will take effect in 2027. That COLA will add about $82 per month to the $2,274.68 average for 70-year-olds. While COLAs help checks keep pace with inflation, they don't erase the gap created by different claiming ages.
 The gap between these two bands reflects the higher concentration of early claimers in their 60s versus the delayers who populate the 70s average.
 Should you claim Social Security in your 60s or 70s?
 The ideal claiming age for you depends on your life expectancy and your financial situation. If you cannot afford to delay your Social Security claim because you don't have another way to cover your bills, applying early is likely your best option, even if you have to settle for a smaller lifetime benefit.
 When this isn't an issue, your ideal claiming age usually comes down to your life expectancy. Those with short life expectancies typically come out ahead by claiming early, while those with longer life expectancies may get more by delaying their application until they qualify for their maximum checks at age 70.
 Married individuals also have to consider how their claiming age will affect their spouse's benefits. They may be eligible to claim a spousal benefit on your work record, but they can only do so if you're claiming a retirement benefit. Talk with your partner to make sure you're both on the same page about when each of you plans to apply for Social Security.
 For more on how Social Security affects your retirement, see this guide .
